question: smb-ai-buying
summary: Small US businesses (5-200 staff) are adopting AI fast by survey standards but are still shallow users: the U.S. Chamber puts small-business AI use at 66% in 2026 (58% in 2025, 23% in 2023), while the Census BTOS - which asks about AI in any business function - puts it at only about 18-20% of employer firms, with adoption rising with firm size and much higher on an employment-weighted basis (32%). In New Jersey's Fed district, 37% of small firms used AI in fall 2025 versus 46% nationally, and 57% of those adopters were still only 'experimenting' (3% fully integrated). The buyer is almost always the owner (69% of SMB tech decision-makers are sole decision-makers, about 58-64% even at 5-99 staff), budgets are set project-by-project or from last year's spend, and planned AI spend is small (72% of firms plan at least $1,000/year). Objections are practical, not philosophical: price and fit lead, followed by data privacy/security, accuracy, integration, time-to-productive and staff training - and the single most common reason given for not adopting is that AI looks 'not applicable' to the business.

findings.finding: Business AI use in the US is between roughly one in six and one in five firms on the Census measure, so a 5-200 staff prospect is more likely to be an AI non-user than a user.
findings.evidence: BTOS data collected Dec 14, 2025-May 3, 2026: overall AI use 'hovered between 17% and 20%', with 19.8% of businesses using AI as of May 3, 2026; 37% of firms with at least 250 employees and 32% of firms with 100-249 employees used AI; 'less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI'; by sector, Information 39.7%, Finance and Insurance 33.9%, Retail Trade about 14% current use.

findings.finding: Adoption measured by employment is nearly double the firm-level rate, and even adopters stay shallow - most use AI in only a few business functions.
findings.evidence: Census working paper on the Nov 17, 2025-Feb 8, 2026 AI supplement: '18% of firms used AI in a business function, rising to 32% on an employment-weighted basis'; adoption expected to reach 22% within six months; among adopting firms '57% of users integrate AI in three or fewer business functions', most commonly Sales and Marketing (52%), Strategy and Business Development (45%) and IT (41%).

findings.finding: A meaningful share of AI use is staff-level rather than firm-level, which is a wedge for a consultant but also a data-governance risk to raise.
findings.evidence: Same Census working paper: 'In 23% (41%, employment-weighted) of firms, workers use AI in work-related tasks'; the evidence 'points to both top-down and bottom-up diffusion channels: worker task use sometimes occurs without formal firm-level adoption, and firm-level adoption sometimes occurs without worker task use'; 66% of users rely on AI solely to augment tasks and AI-related employment decreases occur in only 2% of firms.

findings.finding: New Jersey small businesses lag the national AI adoption rate and most adopters are still experimenting, not integrated.
findings.evidence: Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey 2025 AI module (fielded Sept 3-Nov 14, 2025; 5,248 national responses and 679 from Delaware/New Jersey/Pennsylvania): 37% of Third District firms used AI versus 46% nationally; 57% of District adopters described themselves as 'experimenting with the technology' and 3% had fully integrated it; 44% of District AI users said AI was not important to their core goods and services (vs 37% nationally).

findings.finding: Measured benefits so far are productivity-only; owners are not seeing cost or sales changes, which shapes what they will pay for.
findings.evidence: Same SBCS analysis: 71% of Third District AI-using firms reported AI-related productivity increases, but 'over 70 percent of firms saw no change in labor costs, spending on outside services, quality of goods and/or services, or sales'; nationally 79% reported no employment change, 11% decreases, 10% increases.

findings.finding: The main objections among actual AI users are accuracy, fit, data security/privacy, training time and cost - each cited by more than one in five firms.
findings.evidence: Philadelphia Fed write-up of the national SBCS AI module: 'over 20 percent of firms using AI cite challenges such as accuracy, adapting the technology to business needs, data security and privacy concerns, training time, and costs'. Use case mix in the District: writing/marketing 79%, individual productivity (notetaking, summarizing) 56%, planning or analysis 51%, roughly one-third administrative functions and customer service, 16% process automation, 12% coding.

findings.finding: The U.S. Chamber's series shows a steep, widely publicised adoption curve - but on a broader definition of AI than Census uses, and with methodology not published on the pages I read, so it overstates decision-maker-level adoption of agents.
findings.evidence: 2026 edition (published Oct 2, 2026): '2/3 of small businesses now use AI. (66%), up 8 points from 2025 and nearly 3 times the share using it in 2023 (23%)'; 84% plan to increase their use of technology over the next 2-3 years; 78% of AI users say limiting access would slow growth and 75% say it would hurt the bottom line; 'Six in ten small businesses worry about increased litigation and compliance costs from a patchwork of state privacy and AI laws'; 47% say AI is creating jobs today while 6% say it enables headcount reductions. The report page states no sample size or field dates.

findings.finding: Small businesses overwhelmingly buy AI from outside vendors rather than building it, and most have been using it for a year or less.
findings.evidence: 2025 Chamber report (4th edition, fielded by Teneo Research): 58% of small businesses self-identified as using generative AI (40% in 2024, 23% in 2023); among AI users 'nearly two-thirds (63%) either mostly or entirely rely on externally developed AI tools', 30% a balance, and only 8% take a homegrown approach; 86% adopted generative AI within the past two years and 55% have used it for a year or less; 98% of AI users are working to upskill employees. The report states no sample size or field dates in the sections read.

findings.finding: Competitive pressure, not ROI modelling, is what speeds up small-business AI purchases.
findings.evidence: 2025 Chamber report, asked of businesses that use or plan to use AI: '80% sped up plans for A.I. as a result of their competitors' use of the tech' (24% significantly sped up, 56% somewhat sped up, 18% no impact, 2% somewhat delayed, 0% significantly delayed).

findings.finding: When owners do introduce new technology, they describe it as keeping them level with competitors rather than getting ahead - so 'catching up' is the frame that sells.
findings.evidence: NFIB 2025 survey (N=521 employer respondents): asked whether the technology they introduced put them ahead of the competition, let them stay competitive, or let them catch up, 'Sixty-five percent reported that the new technology introduced allowed them to stay competitive. Fourteen percent reported it let them catch up to the competition, and 11% reported it put them ahead'; 10% said it did not apply. NFIB's own summary: small businesses onboard new tech 'to keep up with the competition rather than find an edge or build a new advantage'.

findings.finding: NFIB's employer survey shows 24% of small employers using AI, with a steep size gradient across exactly our target band and most non-users not planning to start.
findings.evidence: NFIB Small Business and Technology Survey, N=521 employer respondents (the PDF also lists 37 non-employers; field dates are not stated in the PDF): 24% currently use AI (21% of 1-9 employee firms, 24% of 10-24, 28% of 25-49, 48% of 50+); 75% of non-users do not plan to use AI in the next 12 months and 14% plan to soon; 42% are 'not at all familiar' with AI tools for their industry; 63% think AI will be important in their industry in five years but only 56% say so for their own business; uses are communications 29% and marketing/advertising 27%, customer service 9%, process automation 4%; 98% of users report no change in headcount; 30% report higher productivity, 8% lower operating costs.

findings.finding: Vendors and peers, not analysts, are how small businesses first hear about a technology - and staff influence grows with firm size.
findings.evidence: NFIB 2025: asked where they got the idea for purchasing their new or improved technology, 28% said a vendor, 13% another business owner, 13% an employee (8% at 1-9 employees, 13% at 10-24, 21% at 25-49), 37% other. NFIB also reports 20% of non-adopters of new technology said cost was too expensive, 7% said technology is too complicated to adopt, and 5% cited financing cost.

findings.finding: The most common reason firms give for not adopting AI is that it does not apply to their business - a relevance problem, not a trust problem.
findings.evidence: Census BTOS research paper on the first AI supplement (Sept 2023-Feb 2024; about 164,500 businesses in the analysis sample): 'The most common reason for non-adoption is the inapplicability of AI to the business', with remaining options covering cost, skills, data, laws/regulations, privacy/security, bias, technology maturity, and lack of knowledge about capabilities.

findings.finding: The owner is the decision-maker in firms up to about 100 staff; employees shape the choice more as headcount rises.
findings.evidence: SMB Group 2024 SMB Buying Journey Survey (738 completed interviews, June 2024, respondents are finance and technology decision-makers/influencers at firms of 1-2,500 employees): 69% are sole decision-makers, 28% joint, 3% influence-only; sole decision-maker share by size: 60% at 5-9 employees, 62% at 10-19, 64% at 20-49, 58% at 50-99.

findings.finding: Technology budgets are incremental or project-based, and most firms review their stack annually or only as needed - so a purchase usually needs a project trigger.
findings.evidence: SMB Group 2024 (N=735 for the budget question): 33% determine the annual technology budget from 'previous year's spending with adjustments for projected needs', 25% 'aligned with specific project requirements and initiatives', 18% based on profitability, 16% ad hoc, 7% by headcount. Separately (N=738), 41% re-evaluate their technology stack every year, 22% on an as-needed basis, 17% more than once a year, 11% every two years, 8% every three years or more.

findings.finding: Planned AI budgets are small in absolute terms, and privacy/security plus trust in data handling are the top stated obstacles.
findings.evidence: Paychex survey of 1,129 respondents (500+ business owners, 500+ HR leaders), fielded Feb 7-17, 2025, results not weighted: 65% of businesses already use AI; 72% plan to invest at least $1,000 in AI in the next year; 54% cite data privacy and security as a primary challenge to AI adoption, of whom 45% worry about how technology companies use their data and 17% do not trust technology companies with their data; 53% say accurate data would enhance their trust in AI tools; 18% of AI users report difficulties from poor data quality.

findings.finding: What gets a solution onto a small business shortlist is cost-effectiveness, integration and ease of use - features rank lower, and trials are the least-cited reason.
findings.evidence: SMB Group 2024 (N=738, up to 3 responses): most cost-effective 43%, better compatibility/integration with existing systems 34%, easier to use 33%, superior technology and features 31%, easier to customize 24%, easier/faster to deploy 24%, stronger customer service 23%, stronger customer reviews 22%, higher industry analyst ratings 21%, vendor sustainability record 17%, better pre-sales trial/demo 12%. By size: at 5-9 employees cost-effectiveness 52% and ease of use 48%; at 10-19 cost-effectiveness 57%; at 20-49 ease of use 43% and cost-effectiveness 39%.

findings.finding: Buyers say the biggest improvement sellers could make is explaining the business outcome, then showing transparent pricing and taking time to understand requirements.
findings.evidence: SMB Group 2024 (N=738, up to 3 responses), top ways vendors can improve the purchasing experience: better explain how the solution helps improve specific business/technology goals 56%, more transparent pricing information on their site 46%, take more time to understand our requirements 44%, provide a consistent experience across online, mobile and phone channels 39%, better access to phone support 31%, better real-time online chat support 29%, offer better financing options 25%. Top challenges when considering new technology: data privacy and security 47%, difficulty figuring out which solutions will work best 45%, integration 44%, lack of budget 32%, takes too long to get productive 28%, not enough time to try/deploy 25%.

findings.finding: Retention depends on support quality and whether the promised goal was met - the same two factors that justify a recurring care fee.
findings.evidence: SMB Group 2024, factors that strongly influence contract renewal/termination: quality of customer support 52%, degree the solution helped meet goals 52%, solution cost relative to budget 48%, ability to meet contractual obligations/SLAs 44%, vendor responsiveness to feedback 43%, availability of alternatives 33%. Metrics SMBs use to judge success: achievement of specific project goals 51%, increase in productivity 49%, ease of integration 46%.

findings.finding: Food businesses are a live but cautious market: about 39% use AI, one in five is running small pilots, and only about 3% have gone company-wide.
findings.evidence: National Restaurant Association operator survey of 212 restaurant operators, June 18-July 18, 2026: 38.6% of operators use AI tools; 20% are running small-scale pilots and only 3.2% are implementing AI companywide; 42.4% describe their attitude to AI as cautious and 26.2% as excited; top adoption barriers are cost 48.8%, business fit and value 43.8%, workforce/expertise gaps 41.3%, integration 38.8%; AI-specific concerns are complexity 46.1%, cost 43.5%, customer acceptance 41.9%; training and education (56.5%) tops the support operators say would help; 77.9% expect technology, automation, data and AI to be at least moderately critical over the next five years.

findings.finding: In independent insurance agencies, leadership is ahead of staff on AI, and the recommended first step is a written AI policy plus fixing practical workflows.
findings.evidence: Liberty Mutual 2025 Independent Agents at Work Study, more than 1,200 independent agency leaders and staff: more than half of agency employees expressed interest in using AI at work and over one-third reported already integrating AI tools; skepticism persists especially among older staff while younger employees and agency leaders show stronger enthusiasm; the study's three priorities for agency leadership are creating an AI policy (even where AI is not formally adopted, employees may already be using outside tools, raising risk and data-security concerns), starting with practical needs including whether the agency management system already has AI features, and involving employees in selection and implementation.

resources.name: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) - AI data downloads and visualizations
resources.what_it_offers: Biweekly, nationally representative AI-use estimates by state, sector and firm size, including the Nov 17, 2025-Feb 8, 2026 AI supplement covering 15 business functions, tasks and reasons for non-use.
resources.how_to_use_it: Pull the current NJ and sector-level AI-use rates before a prospect meeting so you can say 'firms your size in your sector are at X%' instead of quoting a national headline number.

resources.name: Census working paper CES-WP-26-25 (2026 AI supplement analysis)
resources.what_it_offers: Function-level and task-level adoption detail: 18% of firms vs 32% employment-weighted, 57% of users in three or fewer functions, Sales/Marketing 52%, Strategy 45%, IT 41%, 23% of firms with worker-level AI use.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the function list to frame your offer in the buyer's own language ('intake and document handling', not 'agents'), and to justify starting with one or two functions.

resources.name: Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey - 2025 AI module analysis (Philadelphia Fed, Third District)
resources.what_it_offers: NJ/PA/DE-specific AI adoption, use-case mix, experimentation stage and stated challenges, from 5,248 national and 679 Third District responses fielded Sept 3-Nov 14, 2025.
resources.how_to_use_it: The closest thing to a local benchmark: quote 37% adoption and 57% 'still experimenting' to justify a low-risk pilot rather than a platform sale.

resources.name: U.S. Chamber 'Empowering Small Business: The Impact of Technology' 2026 (and 2025) report
resources.what_it_offers: National small-business AI adoption trend (66% in 2026, 58% in 2025, 23% in 2023), competitive-pressure data, external-vs-homegrown AI sourcing, upskilling behaviour, and privacy-law compliance worry. Neither edition publishes sample size or field dates on the pages I read.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the trend line in outreach content and the '80% sped up because competitors did' finding to open conversations about timing; do not use the headline 66% as your local adoption benchmark.

resources.name: NFIB Small Business and Technology Survey (2025)
resources.what_it_offers: Employer-size breakdowns of AI use (21% at 1-9 staff to 48% at 50+), familiarity, five-year expectations, use cases, headcount effects, where owners get technology ideas, and whether new tech put them ahead or just kept them competitive (N=521 employers; field dates not stated in the PDF).
resources.how_to_use_it: Segment the prospect list by headcount using its size gradient; use the 'vendor 28%, peer 13%' data to justify partner and referral selling over content marketing.

resources.name: SMB Group 2024 SMB Buying Journey Survey
resources.what_it_offers: 738 decision-maker interviews on who decides, how budgets are set, what gets a vendor shortlisted, what buyers want improved in the sales process, and renewal drivers.
resources.how_to_use_it: Turn the pages on shortlist criteria, vendor improvements and renewal factors into your proposal template and discovery script.

resources.name: Paychex small business AI survey (2025) results release
resources.what_it_offers: Stated investment plans (72% plan at least $1,000 in the next year) and detailed trust/privacy objections, with methodology (1,129 respondents, Feb 7-17, 2025, unweighted).
resources.how_to_use_it: Anchor your monthly care fee and pilot fee to these numbers, and lift the trust objections almost verbatim into a one-page data-handling FAQ.

resources.name: NJSBDC (New Jersey Small Business Development Center) one-on-one counseling and workshops
resources.what_it_offers: SBA-funded advising through a state office hosted at Rutgers Business School in Newark and seven regional centers at public colleges and universities; 'Nearly all of our services are provided at no cost'. All clients must file an eRFC (electronic Request for Counseling) form before receiving consulting; once registered, clients 'may request a virtual appointment or be connected with your local Regional Center', which is found by selecting the county where the business is located.
resources.cost: Nearly all services at no cost, per NJSBDC
resources.how_to_use_it: Use free counseling for pricing, contract terms and NJ market feedback as a solo founder. The page does not state which regional center serves Middlesex County, so use its county lookup (inference: nearest center to Milltown not verified).

resources.name: SBA local assistance (SBDC/SCORE/Women's Business Centers by ZIP code)
resources.what_it_offers: SBA states that it and its partner network 'offer free or low-cost counseling and training in your area', searchable by ZIP through the local assistance tool.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the ZIP search to identify the accredited local partners whose client lists overlap your five target verticals - a low-cost route to first prospects and referrals.

resources.name: National Restaurant Association - Research Insight: The Future of Restaurant Technology (2026)
resources.what_it_offers: Operator survey of 212 restaurants on AI use (38.6%), pilot stage (20% small pilots, 3.2% companywide), barriers, AI concerns and the training support operators want. Report published Nov 5, 2026.
resources.cost: Free download from the report page ('Download your copy now!'); whether the download form gates access was not verified
resources.how_to_use_it: Use it to size the restaurant opportunity and to pitch a supervised pilot with staff training rather than a company-wide rollout.

recommendations_for_us: Inference: sell to the owner and expect a one-person decision. SMB Group finds 69% of SMB tech decision-makers are sole decision-makers and NFIB finds owners get technology ideas mainly from vendors (28%) and peers (13%), so founder-led outreach and referral asks will outperform content marketing at this stage.

Inference: lead every pitch with cost and ease of use, not model quality. Cost-effectiveness (43%), integration (34%) and ease of use (33%) top the shortlist criteria while trials and analyst ratings rank lowest (12% and 21%); at 5-9 staff firms cost-effectiveness is 52% and ease of use 48%, and at 10-19 cost-effectiveness is 57%.

Inference: price into a small budget and stage the money. 72% of surveyed businesses plan at least $1,000/year of AI spend (Paychex) and budgets are usually last year's spend adjusted or a specific project, so a modest paid pilot plus a low monthly care fee fits better than an annual platform contract.

Inference: design pilots for two-to-four week time-to-value. 28% of SMBs say new technology 'takes too long to get productive', about a quarter lack time to try it, and 57% of NJ-district adopters are still experimenting - a fast, bounded pilot matches how these buyers actually move.

Inference: make a one-page data handling sheet a standard attachment. 54% of businesses cite data privacy/security as a primary AI challenge, 47% name data privacy as a top challenge when considering new tech, and six in ten worry about a state privacy/AI law patchwork; say plainly where data lives, whether it trains models, and who can see it.

Inference: qualify on relevance before you demo, and sell one function. The Census finds the number-one reason for non-adoption is that AI seems inapplicable, and 57% of adopters use AI in three or fewer functions - so pick phone intake, document intake or back-office follow-up and prove it against a before/after count.

Inference: prioritise 20-200 staff firms and treat sub-20 firms as a later segment. AI use runs 21% at 1-9 staff, 24% at 10-24, 28% at 25-49 and 48% at 50+ in NFIB's data, and Census finds use rising with firm size (32% at 100-249 and 37% at 250+ versus under 20% at firms with four or fewer employees).

Inference: pitch 'keeping up with competitors', not 'getting ahead'. 80% of small businesses that use or plan to use AI sped up their plans because of competitors' use, and owners who introduced new technology mostly said it just let them stay competitive (65%) rather than get ahead (11%).

Inference: build vertical proof first with insurance agencies, restaurants and law firms - the verticals with published buying signals - while home services and property management still need primary interviews because no credible survey was found for them.

Inference: protect renewals with support and goal reviews, because support quality (52%), meeting goals (52%) and cost versus budget (48%) are the strongest renewal drivers; bundle a quarterly metric review into the care fee so the client can see the goal being met.

Inference: for insurance agencies, open with an AI-use policy plus a workflow fix rather than a new platform. The Liberty Mutual study's own recommendations are to write a policy, check what the agency management system already does, and involve staff - which positions us as the implementer who respects those constraints.

pitfalls.pitfall: Quoting '66% of small businesses use AI' as the local buying rate. That figure comes from a Chamber survey with a broad AI definition, no published sample on the report page, and a national sample, while Census BTOS puts function-level use near 18-20% and the Fed's NJ/PA/DE data shows 37% - using the headline number will make your pipeline assumptions and your pitch look inflated.

Assuming benefits are already proven to the buyer. Over 70% of AI-using firms report no change in labor costs, outside-services spending, quality or sales, so pitching headcount reduction or revenue gains as the near-term outcome will not match what comparable owners have experienced.

Leading with a demo or trial. Better pre-sales trial/demo is the least-cited reason a solution gets shortlisted (12%, above only 'other'), while explaining the business goal (56%) and transparent pricing (46%) are the top two improvements buyers ask vendors for.

Fighting the 'not applicable to my business' objection with education. It is the most common stated reason for non-adoption, so long education-led selling wastes cycles; qualify out fast and re-approach when a specific workflow breaks.

Ignoring staff-level AI use already in the building. 23% of firms (41% employment-weighted) report workers using AI in work-related tasks, and the data show worker-level use sometimes occurs without formal firm-level adoption; the insurance-agency research adds that even in agencies that have not formally adopted AI, employees may already be using outside tools with client information - a governance gap you should surface, not step around.

Treating restaurants as a fast-moving AI market. Only 3.2% of operators have company-wide AI, 42.4% describe themselves as cautious, and cost, fit and complexity are the top concerns - expect small pilots with tight scope and staff training included.

caveats: Definitions differ across sources: Census BTOS asked about AI 'in producing goods or services' until Nov 17, 2025 and then broadened the question to 'in any business function', so pre- and post-November 2025 figures are not a like-for-like series (inference from the stated wording change); the Chamber asks about generative AI/any AI platform; NFIB lists consumer tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, Grammarly, Canva). Percentages are therefore not comparable across surveys.
Reported adoption reflects self-identification, not deployment depth: 57% of Third District adopters operate in three or fewer functions, and only about 3% describe themselves as fully integrated.

Several sources are vendor- or sponsor-funded (Paychex, SMB Group, Liberty Mutual via trade press, and the National Restaurant Association research, whose report page lists DoorDash Direct as presenting sponsor and PayPal as supporting sponsor); Paychex states its results were not weighted, and the SMB Group sample spans 1-2,500 employees, so its size bands should be read per band rather than as one 'SMB' average.

The U.S. Chamber's 2025 and 2026 editions (2025 fielded by Teneo Research) do not publish sample size or field dates on the pages or PDF sections I read; both are rated Medium for that reason even though they are the most widely quoted numbers in this space.
The NFIB 2025 PDF publishes sample sizes (N=521 employer respondents, plus 37 non-employers) but not field dates, and nfib.com article pages returned HTTP 403, so no exact field period is asserted.
No single survey covers the 5-200 employee band exactly; Census and Fed size bands split at 4/5, 19/20, 99/100 and 249/250, so figures for our segment are interpolations between published bands.
Liberty Mutual's insurance study is cited through Insurance Business magazine because the primary research page returned HTTP 403; treat those qualitative findings as directional only.

The Census non-adoption reasons come from the 2023-24 supplement cycle (published 2024); the newer Nov 2025-Feb 2026 supplement asks about reasons for non-use again but I did not retrieve those tabulations.
The restaurant figures come from the Association's press release, not from the report PDF, which requires submitting a download form I did not complete.
data_gaps: ABA 2024 Legal Technology Survey AI report (commonly cited as 24.1% adoption at 2-9 lawyer firms and 17.7% for solos) could not be opened: americanbar.org returned HTTP 403 on every attempt, including the press release. No law-firm adoption figure is therefore asserted in findings.

Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses AI spending data (reported in October 2026 as 73% of owners spending $100 or less per month on AI, 86% of 2,474 alumni using AI) could not be verified: axios.com and goldmansachs.com both returned HTTP 403.
American Express 2025 small business AI study (security 23%, distrust of accuracy 21% among non-users) could not be fetched; not cited.

U.S. Chamber 2026 and 2025 reports: sample size and field dates are not stated on the report page or in the PDF sections I read; secondary summaries mention 3,732 firms surveyed July 23-August 6, 2026 for the 2026 edition, which I could not confirm on a primary page.

No verified New Jersey-specific AI adoption percentage: the Philadelphia Fed notes state-level SBCS samples in the Third District were too small to report individually, and I did not pull NJ from the BTOS state tables.
No credible survey found on AI buying by home-services contractors or by property-management firms; that part of the target list still needs primary interviews.
SCORE Princeton's chapter page returned HTTP 403, so its free-mentoring terms are referenced only through SBA's general local-assistance statement.
Liberty Mutual/Agent for the Future primary research page returned HTTP 403; the insurance findings rely on trade-press reporting of that study.
NJSBDC's page says to pick the nearest regional center by county but does not list which center covers Middlesex County, so proximity for Milltown is unconfirmed.
The National Restaurant Association report PDF was not downloaded (it requires submitting a form), so the restaurant figures rest on the press release only.
